item.title: Inside 'Grand Theft Auto VI'—and the Real-Life Florida Locations That Inspired It
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Set to be released on November 19, 2026, Grand Theft Auto VI is expected to be the most profitable piece of media ever created. Pre-sale estimates suggest the game has made a staggering $476 million in revenue already. Dreamt up by Scottish developers Rockstar Games, the GTA series has been big business for some time now. The previous instalment, Grand Theft Auto V has reportedly made a whopping $11 billion since its release in 2013. Not bad for a game in which you essentially steal cars and shoot guns. If you haven’t played the games, you should know that they take place in a sort of shadow version of the US, with each game taking place in a new city inspired by a real-world counterpart. For me, they’ve been a fascinating companion to my travels in America. When I’m in New York, walking among towering skyscrapers, I can’t help but be reminded of Liberty City, the location of 2001’s dark and atmospheric Grand Theft Auto III. On holiday in Los Angeles, driving along the Pacific Coast Highway, the long, ocean-view roads of GTA V’s Los Santos were front of mind. It works both ways. Red Dead Redemption 2, an open-world cowboy game released by Rockstar between GTAs V and VI, is perhaps the most immersive video game to date. In it, you can wander everywhere from dry, open deserts to lush forests where you can kick back with your horse, camp, and look for rare herbs and flowers. For me, it’s inspired trips to the deserts of the American Southwest and served as an interesting entry point into learning about US history. Now when I’m abroad, I’m thinking of these games, but also learning more about the real-world events and cultures that inspired them. It’s a full-circle moment that only enriches my travels. These gaming vacations, or ‘gami-vacations’, are becoming increasingly popular. Fans are traveling to Tokyo to visit real-life locations from the Yakuza series and role-playing classic Persona 5, to Paris to see locations featured in the Assassin’s Creed series, to the Pacific Northwest to soak up the vibes of zombie classic Day Gone, and to Iceland to walk dramatic black sand beaches like those in the Hellblade series. “Santa Monica, the Sunset Strip, and Griffith Observatory from GTA V,” one Reddit user replied to a post asking about video game locations fans wanted to visit in real life. “Old town Tallinn feels like a very fairytale environment to me. If you went in winter, it would feel like a set from Assassin's Creed,” suggests another Redditor. Far from being confined to their rooms, crouched over consoles, gamers are increasingly inspired to get out into the world. It’s a beautiful tradition, and one that GTA 6 looks set to continue. Set in the fictional state of Leonida, GTA 6 is set to be the franchise’s largest map to date. With six key locations, there promises to be something for every type of traveller. Here’s what you need to know, along with the real-world inspirations for each game location. “We’re a long way from the ‘80s, but Vice City is still the sun and fun capital of America,” reads Rockstar’s official guide to GTA VI’s base of operations, Vice City. As fans are aware, the new game returns to the setting of the 2002 release, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. Set in the 1980s, that game borrowed pretty heavily from the story of Brian De Palma’s brace of crime films Scarface and Carlito’s Way, giving players the ability to control one Tommy Vercetti as he rises from the streets to build a narcotics empire. As expected, disco, perms, neon signs and flared trousers were the order of the day. Updated for 2026, GTA VI’s Vice City is a modern cityscape full of high-rises, trendy rooftop bars, nightclubs. and more. It sounds pretty idyllic, but this being GTA, there’s a shadier side, too. “When the sun fades and the neon glows, everyone has something to gain—and more to lose,” the official longline reads. The recent Netflix preview of the upcoming game gave us a bit more insight into the locale, including shots of BASE jumping from city bridges, a jewelry store robbery and subsequent high-speed escape, and a shootout through a drug den in a down-on-its-luck neighbourhood. In other words, as the main large city in the game, it looks like there’s plenty to keep Vice City residents occupied—on both sides of the law. Inspiration: While Rockstar doesn’t explicitly explain that ‘game location X equals real world location Y’, it’s pretty obvious that Vice City is based on South Florida’s party capital, Miami. Despite the criminal element of Vice City, the real-world city has been keen to play on the connection. A New York Times story suggests the city is keen to embrace its fictional twin due to a drastic drop in real-world crime recently. Which is, of course, great news for tourists. For the full GTA experience, you can enjoy Miami’s beaches, bars, and car culture, alongside iconic EDM nightspots like Club Space and E11EVEN Miami. In Leonida Keys, the dress code is casual and the bars are loaded. “Life in this tropical archipelago isn’t flashy, but it’s easy,” runs the official description. In game, the Keys look like an ideal place to hit pristine tropical waters for a dive, jet ski, or scuba trip. Naturally, there seems to be a strong party boat presence too, with a Spring Break vibe. While we’re sure some absolute in-game carnage will take place there, at present, it actually looks like quite a nice place to unwind and escape the more criminal elements of the game’s plot. Inspiration: The obvious IRL comp here is Key West, nestled at the very southern tip of Florida. In fact, here you can see the southernmost point in the continental US, just 90 miles from Cuba as the crow flies. As well as a plethora of luxury hotels, casual bars, and seafood spots, you can kick back on white beaches, or enjoy a glass-bottomed boat tour. For a break from all of this, you can visit the Hemingway Home, where Ernest Hemingway finished books including A Farewell to Arms and To Have and Have Not—that is, when he wasn’t out big-game fishing. The house is home to the first-ever swimming pool built in the Keys, as well as descendants of Hemingway’s famous six-toed cats. Fans don’t know much about GTA 6’s Grassrivers yet, although the official synopsis does suggest some intrigue: “You never know what lies beneath the surface of this primordial expanse. The gators may be the most famous attraction, but there are far deadlier predators and weirder discoveries among the mangroves.” So far, all we’ve seen is an airboat tour and a birdwatching tower, suggesting a heavy emphasis on encounters with the natural world. Watch this space. Inspiration: Clearly inspired by the Florida Everglades, Grassrivers will surely have a feel and flavor all of its own. The real Everglades has a rich cultural history. Yes, there are airboat tours catered to tourists during which you can spot ‘gators and learn all about the invasive pythons that are terrorising the ecosystem. And yes, you will be able to try deep-fried gator afterwards. But the real treasure is traditional foods like thick and chewy fry bread, swamp cabbage, or sofkee, a thin porridge made from corn. And, at the Ah-Tah-Thi-Ki Museum near Fort Lauderdale in the north of the Everglades, you can learn about the Seminole nation, a group made up of Native Americans moving south to escape the British, mixed with escaped formerly enslaved peoples from the area’s plantations. If GTA 6 were represented on an old-timey naval map, Port Gellhorn a “failed resort on the edge of the map" might be marked “here be monsters.” We know very little about the area yet, except for the fact that it’s rooted in poverty, with locals pushed to extremes to make ends meet. According to Rockstar, “Cheap motels, shut-down attractions and empty strip malls won’t bring the tourists back, but there’s a new economy in this once-popular vacation spot. It’s fuelled by malt liquor, painkillers and truck-stop energy drinks. Jump on a dirt bike and hold onto your wallet.” In other words, it sounds like a great place for a video game, less so for a holiday. Inspiration: Again, Rockstar hasn’t been open about which area of Florida Port Gellhorn is based on, but fans and Florida locals think it takes inspiration from Panama City and the surrounding areas in the Florida Panhandle. Off the beaten track of most holidays, Panama City nevertheless has a strong reputation for seafood and water sports. Given its deepwater port, there’s also a strong maritime history. St Andrews State Park might be your best bet for snorkelling, swimming, kayaking and a calm and safe designated tidal pool. Ambrosia sounds, possibly, like the least appealing locale in GTA 6. It’s reportedly a factory town, overseen by vicious biker gangs. “In the heart of Leonida, American industry and old-school values still reign supreme – whatever the cost. The Allied Crystal sugar refinery provides the jobs, while the local biker gang provides almost everything else,” runs Rockstar’s official primer on the place. The Netflix preview didn’t help. We saw a shootout in a dilapidated house, backyard wrestling, and possibly some mud-wrestling too. Mark this one as the biggest unknown of the game. Inspiration: Florida locals think Ambrosia is based on Clewiston, Florida and the surrounding agricultural area around Lake Okeechobee. The main crop here is sugar, with Clewiston known as "America's Sweetest Town.” The irony in the in-game depiction is pretty obvious here, but the IRL location is well worth a visit if you’re a fan of fishing, with the local largemouth bass on Lake Okeechobee a particularly sought-after prize. Mount Kalaga National Park looks like a truly beautiful in-game location, teeming with wildlife and activities from bicycle riding to kayaking. What’s not to love? Well, this bucolic utopia may actually prove to be too good to be true. In the Netflix preview, a televised advert for the ‘Prairie Sandwich’ seemed to take place in the park, suggesting that rather than enjoying the park’s animals in their natural habitat, your main goal might actually be to shoot them. If so, hunting will be an interesting addition to the game, and one that worked well in Red Dead Redemption 2. Of course, players will probably be able to opt out of the bloodshed and just enjoy a nice stroll among the trees instead. Here’s hoping. Inspiration: While there’s no one-for-one comp for Mount Kalaga National Park, the Southern US States in particular are well known for their stunning national parks. Fans think this one takes inspiration from North Carolina’s Table Rock Mountain, Georgia’s Providence Canyon State Park, and the Suwannee River, which runs through Georgia and Florida. Whatever the real inspiration, if you are visiting Florida, it’s a reminder to get off the beaten path and out of the cities into lovingly preserved wild areas.

item.title: IDEA: Why Travel Vlogging Is Popular With Backpackers
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Travel vlogging has evolved from a niche hobby into a mainstream way for backpackers to document and share their journeys. What began as a few adventurers uploading shaky smartphone footage to YouTube has become a sophisticated form of travel storytelling, with editing techniques, narrative arcs, and millions of engaged viewers. For independent travelers, the ability to capture and share experiences in real time has fundamentally changed how people plan trips, discover destinations, and connect with other adventurers around the world. The democratization of content creation tools means anyone with a smartphone and basic equipment can produce travel videos rivaling professional productions from a few years ago. Whether hiking through Southeast Asia, island hopping in the Caribbean, or exploring remote mountain villages, documenting your journey has never been easier. Understanding the landscape of travel vlogging, from equipment choices to storytelling approaches, can help you decide if this form of documentation fits your travel style. Gear options range from simple smartphone setups to dedicated vlogging cameras designed for mobile creators and adventurers. Travel vlogging emerged as YouTube matured and mobile technology improved. Early vloggers faced technical limitations: heavy cameras, poor stabilization, limited battery life, and complicated editing workflows. Today's landscape is different. Smartphones have become powerful filming devices, and specialized equipment is lighter, more affordable, and easier to use than before. The appeal of travel vlogging goes beyond vanity or social media metrics. Many backpackers use vlogging as a way to process their experiences, create a visual diary, and maintain connections with friends and family back home. Filming forces you to observe your surroundings more carefully, notice details you might miss, and think about how to communicate a place's essence to others. This reflective aspect of content creation can deepen your travel experience rather than detract from it. The audience for travel content has also expanded dramatically. People planning trips are increasingly turning to travel vlogs for authentic, on-the-ground perspectives that traditional tourism websites don't provide. A well-produced vlog showing the reality of a budget hostel, local market, or hiking trail offers genuine value to future travelers. This creates a positive feedback loop where creators feel motivated to produce higher-quality content, attracting larger audiences and more aspiring vloggers. One legitimate concern about travel vlogging is experiencing destinations through a camera lens rather than living in the moment. The pressure to capture every single sunset, meal, and scenic viewpoint can turn travel from an absorbing experience into a series of photo opportunities. Finding balance calls for deliberate choices about when to film and when to be present. Experienced travel vloggers develop personal guidelines about filming versus exploration time. Some set aside certain hours for content creation and leave the rest of the day camera-free. Others film only certain activities or locations, letting spontaneous experiences remain undocumented. The key is recognizing that not every moment needs to be captured. Some of your most meaningful travel experiences may never appear in a video, and that's perfectly acceptable. Ask permission before filming people, respect regional customs and photography restrictions, and avoid sharing your accommodation or live location publicly. The physical and mental energy required for consistent vlogging should be considered. Filming, transferring footage, editing, and uploading require time and concentration. On a long backpacking trip, this workload can become exhausting, especially when traveling through areas with unreliable internet. Many successful travel creators build in rest days specifically for content production, treating it as separate from travel rather than something that happens simultaneously. Equipment Considerations For Budget Travelers The equipment question often stops potential travel vloggers before they begin. The good news is you don't need expensive gear to produce watchable travel content. A modern smartphone is enough to start. Most current phones shoot in 4K, offer reasonable stabilization, and have intuitive camera apps. The learning curve is minimal, and the barrier to entry is essentially zero if you already own a phone. As your skills develop and your audience grows, you might consider supplementary equipment. Smartphone gimbals provide smoother footage and more professional-looking pans and tracking shots. Portable tripods enable hands-free filming and creative angles. External microphones improve audio quality, often more important to viewers than video quality. Portable lighting kits help in poorly lit environments. Costs vary; these items don't have to be expensive, and each serves a specific purpose without being essential for beginners. Add accessories only when they solve a specific filming problem. Storage and backup systems deserve attention. Traveling with large amounts of video footage requires reliable external storage and ideally a backup system. Losing weeks of footage to a corrupted memory card or stolen hard drive is a genuine risk for travel creators. Cloud backup services require internet access but provide an additional layer of security. Planning your storage strategy before you leave home prevents frustration and potential loss of irreplaceable content. The most successful travel vlogs prioritize storytelling over production quality. Viewers connect with authentic narratives, genuine reactions, and honest reflections far more than they do with polished cinematography or expensive equipment. Some of the most popular travel channels feature relatively simple production values but compelling stories about overcoming difficulties, discovering unexpected places, or connecting with local communities. Effective travel vlogging requires identifying the narrative thread of your journey. What story are you trying to tell? Is it about budget travel, adventure and challenge, cultural discovery, or personal transformation? Your narrative focus shapes which moments you capture, how you edit them, and what message emerges. A clear narrative makes your vlogs more interesting and gives viewers a reason to follow your channel beyond watching pretty scenery. Authenticity resonates with travel audiences. Viewers appreciate creators who show difficult moments, failed plans, uncomfortable situations, and genuine struggles of travel, not just the highlight reel. Showing yourself getting lost, dealing with food poisoning, or facing frustrating interactions with local bureaucracy makes your content relatable and honest. These moments often generate more engagement and loyalty than perfect travel sequences. Travel vlogging creates opportunities to connect with other travelers, before and after your trip. Viewers often become inspired to visit the same destinations, and many travel vloggers report meeting audience members in person during their travels. These connections transform vlogging from a one-way broadcast into a genuine community experience. Interacting with your audience through comments, messages, and social media builds loyalty and provides valuable feedback on what content resonates. Many travel creators use their platforms to crowdsource recommendations, ask for advice about upcoming destinations, and share viewer stories. This united approach makes the audience feel invested in the creator's journey rather than passive consumers. The travel vlogging community is remarkably supportive. Experienced creators share advice with newcomers, partner on projects, and celebrate each other's successes. This team-oriented spirit embodies the broader backpacking culture, where travelers help each other meet challenges and share hard-won knowledge about destinations and routes. Travel vlogging is a meaningful way for backpackers to document journeys, connect with communities, and contribute to collective knowledge of independent travel. Whether as a casual hobby or serious creative pursuit, the fundamentals remain the same: capture real moments, tell compelling stories, and balance documentation with presence. Today's tools and apps make it easier than ever to share your adventures, and audiences for travel content continue to grow. If you're considering adding vlogging to your travel experience, start simple, focus on storytelling, and allow your passion for exploration to shine through. This story was published in partnership with Insta360.

item.title: IDEA: Using an eSIM in Italy: A Practical Guide From Our Recent Trip
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
When we touched down in Rome, Kel was still shaking off the last bits of work from home. Sorting out mobile data for Italy had slipped down her to-do list. She wanted to keep one foot in the world: work emails, news updates, and the scores from her favorite teams. So, our first order of business in Rome was picking up a 20 GB Nomad eSIM Italy plan for $25. Once we checked into our hotel, I walked her through the setup on her phone. This was my fifth time in Italy since 1998, and Rome was just the beginning. We had a string of stops ahead: Sorrento, Positano, Naples, and finally Sicily. Kel wanted data for the whole trip, including the days we'd spend getting from one place to the next. If you're thinking about an eSIM for Italy, ask yourself: Will it work on your phone? Will it last the length of your trip? And how much data do you actually use when you're away from Wi-Fi? When Mobile Data Comes in Handy in Italy I can spend a good part of an afternoon roaming around Rome without much planning. On a travel day, though, I want to pull up the ticket, check where we're supposed to be, and let the next hotel know if we're running late. Our route included a high-speed train, coastal ferries, a flight from Naples to Palermo, and a regional train from Palermo to Catania. Each travel day provided a new set of tickets to juggle, directions to follow, and addresses to keep straight. If you're putting together a trip like ours without a rental car, pay attention to the gaps between Wi-Fi. That's when you'll need to verify a ferry terminal, figure out which train station you need, or pull up the map for those last few blocks to your hotel, bags in tow. I remember arriving in Florence by train in 2018, seeing the taxi line in the rain, and pulling up the walk to my hostel on Google Maps. Even on occasions when we stayed put, mobile data came in handy. If I'm mapping out a day around food, as I did eating in Bologna, I'll save a handful of places in the same neighborhood. Being able to check opening hours or pivot to a new lunch spot on the fly makes it easier to follow your appetite instead of a fixed plan. When I asked Kel what she ended up using the eSIM for, she said she used it to check Instagram and X on train rides. And at restaurants, she liked being able to quietly look up unfamiliar Italian words on the menu instead of asking for my help with translations. What To Check Before Buying an eSIM for Italy An eSIM is a digital SIM you install on your phone. A travel eSIM gives you access to a mobile plan without buying and swapping in a physical SIM card. On a compatible dual-SIM phone, you can use the travel line for mobile data while keeping your regular line available if you need it. If you have an iPhone, Apple's guide to traveling with an eSIM shows you how to check whether your phone is unlocked before you buy a plan. Check your exact phone model and whether it's unlocked. You need a phone that supports eSIM and can accept a plan from another carrier. Check both before paying. If you're setting up a plan for someone else, do this on their phone. Two phones that look alike can have different carrier restrictions. Count your days and check when the clock starts. Look at how long the plan lasts once it starts and how soon after purchase you have to activate it. Those are two different clocks. A seven-day plan might cover a week in Rome, but for a trip like ours I'd look for one that lasts through the final transfer to the airport. When you count, check the arrival and departure dates. Think about what you'll use away from Wi-Fi. Looking up directions, messaging, and opening booking confirmations are different from watching video, uploading photos, or using your phone as a hotspot for a laptop. Before guessing how much you'll need, look at which apps use the most mobile data on your phone at home. Then think about which of those you'll use on the road. If you tend to back up photos every evening, for instance, you can do that on the hotel Wi-Fi. Decide if you need regular calls or texts. The Italy plans discussed here are for mobile data. Apps such as WhatsApp can use that connection, but the travel plan won't give you an Italian phone number for ordinary calls or texts. If you keep your home line enabled for things like bank verification texts, check how your carrier handles calls, texts, and roaming abroad. We paid $25 for 20 GB in Rome in October 2026. As of this writing, the Nomad eSIM plans for Italy range from 1 GB for seven days to 50 GB for 30 days. The 20 GB plan is listed with 30 days of validity, and unlimited options are available for stays of three, five, seven, or ten days. For a trip like ours, I'd start with the 30-day plans and then think honestly about how often I'd be away from Wi-Fi. Kel made good use of hotel Wi-Fi during afternoon breaks and after dinner. By the time we rolled into Catania, I think she still had more than half of her 20 GB left. If we traveled the same way again, I'd probably go for a smaller plan next time. If you're looking at an unlimited option, check how much high-speed data it includes each day and what happens to speeds after you use it. Nomad eSIM offers plans for more than 200 destinations. Our trip stayed within Italy, including Sicily. If your trip continues into another country, compare the Italy plan with Nomad eSIM's Europe plans or the Nomad Pass subscription, and make sure your chosen plan covers every stop on your itinerary. If you're new to Nomad eSIM and want to try it before buying a plan, you can redeem a free 1 GB trial in the app. It's available in 80 destinations, including Italy, and lasts three days once activated. At the time of writing, Nomad eSIM has a 4.3 out of 5 rating on Trustpilot based on more than 48,000 reviews. Its iPhone app has a 4.8 out of 5 rating in the U.S. App Store. If you're saving it for arrival, wait until you're less than 15 days away from arriving in Italy. The trial starts automatically 15 days after redemption if you haven't used it by then. We bought Kel's eSIM after landing in Rome, but if I were helping someone prep for the same trip now, I'd check the phone and read through the installation steps at home, where you've got time and a steady connection. Kel's on an iPhone 18 Pro. Once we settled on the 20 GB plan, we downloaded the Nomad eSIM app, and I walked her through the install right in the app. - Install it while you're online. Use Wi-Fi to follow the instructions for your plan. With Nomad eSIM, you may be able to install it in the app or via a QR code. If you're using a QR code, have it open on another screen if your phone needs to scan it. Give the new line a name you'll recognize in Settings, such as "Italy data." - Check the activation instructions. If you buy your Italy eSIM before leaving home, keep two dates in mind. For a paid Nomad eSIM Italy plan, you have 60 days from purchase to activate it. If you haven't activated it by then, the plan starts automatically. The plan's validity period starts when you activate it. Check your order email for instructions, since some plans require a manual step. - Select the travel line for mobile data. Once you're ready to use the eSIM, turn it on and select it as your cellular or mobile data line. Follow Nomad eSIM's instructions for enabling data roaming on the travel line. If you keep your home line active for calls or texts, turn off data roaming on that line. On an iPhone, turn off Allow Cellular Data Switching to keep mobile data on the travel line. - Test it before leaving Wi-Fi behind. Briefly turn off Wi-Fi and open a fresh webpage or search for a place in your maps app. If it doesn't load, check which line is selected for data and whether roaming is enabled on the travel line. Once it works, you can turn Wi-Fi back on. Before our next trip to Italy, I'd download offline maps for each place we're staying and save all our tickets and booking confirmations so I can pull them up even without a cell signal. For ferries, I'd save the departure points and boarding instructions. On days with train trips, I'd jot down the station names and check how the operator wants to see our tickets. Spending a few minutes on this at home can save scrambling at the station with your bags. When I'm traveling with Kel, I'd make sure we both have the next hotel address and any tickets we'll need in case we split up for a few hours. I'd also check my data balance a few days into the trip. That's usually early enough to catch things like automatic photo uploads eating up more data than I planned. Nomad eSIM sends email and push alerts at 60% and 80% of your allowance, and you can check what's left anytime in the app under Manage. I still like to leave room to get a little lost in Rome. I just like knowing I can find my way back when I'm ready. Nomad eSIM sponsored this article. Kel and I bought her eSIM ourselves in Rome, and I wrote this guide based on our experience during the trip.

item.title: American to double down on LAX hub with more flights, promises 'compelling offering'
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
American Airlines is planning to add more flights from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), as part of a “gradual build” at its West Coast hub. The Fort Worth-based carrier said it's about to add more LAX service to its schedule, with a focus on places executives describe as “important markets.” It’s not clear whether that means entirely new routes or more frequent service on existing ones. But either way, it comes after a long stretch where American seemed to focus far more of its attention on other parts of the country. After the pandemic, the airline doubled down on its Sun Belt hubs, fortifying its strongholds in Dallas, Charlotte and Miami. More recently, American reignited a longstanding Chicago turf war with United Airlines when it rapidly reinstated flying at O’Hare International Airport (ORD). It looks like LAX will be its next project. “We’re going to grow," American chief commercial officer Nat Pieper said, speaking this week at an industry conference. "We’re going to tailor a schedule to the local market." It won’t happen overnight. American has a smaller presence today in Southern California than it did several years ago. This year, the carrier will operate about 32% fewer flights than it did in 2019, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium. That’s a significant drop-off at LAX, which is one of the nation’s most competitive airports — and the only where each of the “big three” legacy carriers operates a hub. By contrast, top L.A. rival Delta Air Lines has solidified its place as the airport’s top carrier, and plans operate its largest-ever schedule there next year. United Airlines has also signaled it has future growth aspirations at LAX. Speaking earlier this year, United’s top network planner, Patrick Quayle, lamented the fact that the airport is United’s only hub where there’s another airline with a larger presence. “I don’t like being No. 2,” Quayle said during a company event at LAX in March. “And so I will, today, put Delta on notice here in L.A. — we will be No. 1, as well.”' How American plans to grow in L.A. So where does that leave American? Pieper said the carrier needs to start by catering more to local Los Angeles customers — not just using the airport as a hub to route connecting traffic. Doing that, he acknowledged, will likely require AA to offer a longer list of unique destinations. Today, for instance, the carrier only serves four long-haul cities from LAX: London, Tokyo, Sydney and Auckland. “People don’t only want to fly domestically. They want to go to Latin America. They want to go to Europe. They want to go to Asia,” Pieper said on stage this week at the Skift Aviation Forum in New York. “We need to be able to serve that with our own airplanes.” United is clearly following that formula. The carrier already serves more than a half-dozen transpacific destinations from Southern California — and will expand next year with a new route to Osaka. Delta, for its part, is also pointing to LAX as a linchpin of its Pacific growth aspirations, having launched nonstops to Hong Kong and Melbourne within the past year. New flights to Manila will begin in 2027. Delta’s Los Angeles growth is also thanks, in part, to massive infrastructure investments the carrier has made at the hub which, among other things, is the only airport that's home to two Delta One Lounges. American’s LAX digs, meanwhile, are still a construction zone. The carrier had to consolidate its presence at the airport last year to make way for a rebuild of the airport's Terminal 5. American will grow at a "gradual" pace, Pieper said, until its LAX facilities are "ready to roll." That's expected to happen in late 2028, at which point the carrier will have access to 30 gates. “Our facility will be as good as anybody’s,” he said. That, along with more flights — plus connectivity to American's Pacific partners like Qantas and Japan Airlines— have the airline more bullish about its hub that's grabbed far fewer headlines in recent years. “You combine all those things together,” Pieper added, “I think we’re going to have a compelling offering there.” Related reading:

item.title: IDEA: What You Need to Know About Japanese Knives
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
The popularity of Japanese knives in home and commercial kitchens has exploded in the last few years, and for good reason: A lot of them outperform their Western counterparts in kitchen tests. Western-style knives are bulkier, all-purpose kitchen tools—years ago, it would be common for many chefs to use the heavy bolster near the heel of the blade to crack open a can of tomatoes during service. Japanese knives (and Japanese-style knives produced by manufacturers elsewhere) are designed with precision cuts in mind and usually have a specific purpose. However, because they’re designed with that specificity in mind, it can be tricky to know what you need and what you’ll use. Thankfully, we’ve reviewed a wide variety of Japanese-style knives for Bon Appétit and have assembled a roundup to help you identify exactly what your kitchen needs. While there are more styles of Japanese knives than those listed here, these options have all been thoroughly tested, giving us the confidence to speak to each knife’s utility. Before we jump into specific styles, however, it’s useful to give a quick rundown on some of the broad strokes of what makes a Japanese-style knife unique. Many Japanese knives are designed for push cuts or pull-through slicing rather than the rocking chop of a heavy Western chef’s knife. They tend to have a straighter edge than their Western counterparts, making them slightly less adept at speeding through a mince of herbs, but more precise in their cuts. Most Japanese-style knives also feature a sheep’s-foot tip that curves down to the point, giving the user more control over fine-point work. Japanese knives are often made with a harder steel than their Western counterparts. Harder steel helps a knife’s edge retain sharpness, which lets manufacturers use steeper sharpening angles for a finer edge. This helps most Japanese knives slice more delicately than Western knives, though harder steel can chip on material like ice or bone. Traditional Japanese-style knives are only sharpened on one side, giving them a much finer edge than the 50/50 bevel of Western-style knives that are sharpened on both sides. Some modern Japanese knife makers have pivoted to a 50/50 style bevel for ease of sharpening; however, when you’re shopping, you’ll encounter plenty of knives with 70/30 bevel with the inside edge (the left edge for a right-handed knife) sharpened at a steeper angle. A 70/30 bevel is easier to maintain than a single-bevel but offers a sharper edge than a 50/50 bevel. Many traditional Japanese kitchen knives feature a wa-style handle—an octagonal wood handle that envelops a hidden knife tang (the metal part of the knife that connects to the handle). Wa-style handles help keep knives lighter and nimbler, while many Western-style knives use full-tang construction, adding weight and heft to the blade. Many modern Japanese knife makers, though, combine full-tang knife handles with Japanese blade shapes to create a hybrid-style knife that’s both durable and adept at slicing. The gyuto, or Japanese chef’s knife, originated in Japan in the early 1900s, when French cooking began to gain popularity in a rapidly modernizing country. This knife style took cues from the traditional French chef’s knife and combined them with elements of traditional Japanese knife making. The resulting Japanese take on a chef’s knife was primarily designed for slicing meat, though it also features a curved edge that makes it easy to chop herbs. Compared to a Western chef’s knife, the gyuto has a straighter blade and a drop point tip with a lower overall profile. This is primarily designed so that the user can place the knife’s tip on the cutting board and draw it through food, taking advantage of the gyuto’s sharp edge and thin blade for precision slicing. But while the gyuto excels at slicing meat, its general shape makes it an overall great pick to anchor your knife collection, and many home cooks opt for a gyuto as their daily driver over a traditional chef’s knife. We’ve long been fans of the gyuto fan here at Bon Appétit, with MAC’s Professional Hollow Ground Chef’s Knife topping our chef’s knife review for years. For a wicked sharp, more traditional option, we really like the Kazan Arare by Shibata gyuto, which impressed us so much we had to give it its own review. Increasingly common as a part of brands’ knife sets, the santoku knife is a relatively modern knife shape, first appearing in the 1940s or so. Nicknamed the three virtues knife, the santoku draws on the gyuto, nakiri, and deba to create a well-rounded utility knife that’s great for cutting meat, fish, and vegetables. Typically, these knives feature a pretty steep sheep’s-foot tip for precision point work, a tall heel for push cuts, and just enough curve for pull-through slicing and rock-chopping. A santoku knife is great for well-rounded utility work—think cutting cheese and an apple for a snack, slicing leftover roasted chicken to make a sandwich, or dicing an onion for a curry. Typically, we like a santoku knife that’s between six and seven inches, so it contrasts with the longer gyuto. Our favorite overall model is the MAC Professional Santoku Knife, but if you’d like a razor-sharp version with a traditional wa-style handle, we love the Kazan Ginsan Nashiji Santoku. Nakiri knives have a straight edge and a sturdy spine, specifically designed for chopping vegetables. Sometimes referred to as a vegetable cleaver, the nakiri excels at push cuts, making it great for both matchsticking carrots and breaking down tough-skinned squash. Since most gyutos feature thin blades and fine edges, the nakiri also holds a spot in the Japanese knife lineup as a tougher, heavier knife for more demanding tasks. Traditional nakiri knives may also feature a blunt, rounded tip, which can be rotated against the cutting board to create a smooth, chopping motion. The Tojiro DP Damascus Nakiri is by far our overall favorite tested nakiri knife for its extremely sharp edge and overall balance, but it’s also pricey. We also really like the Tojiro Classic nakiri, though it can have stock issues due to its popularity and price point. The deba knife is a traditional Japanese knife designed for fish butchery. Unlike a Western fillet knife, which is designed to be flexible and nimble, the deba is a heavy, sturdy blade with a thick spine that gives the heel of the blade a cleaver-like feel. But a deba knife is also designed for precision slicing, and it usually features a traditional single-bevel edge. That single-bevel edge allows the knife to come to a finer point than a double-bevel edge, and the sheep’s-foot tip adds to the deba knife’s ability to portion out delicate fish fillets as well. We haven’t tested deba knives because they require a bit of knowledge and skill to use them for breaking down whole fish, but if you’re intrigued by the shape and want a cleaver-like knife for your kitchen, the Seki Mago Roku Deba from Kai is an affordable, solid option. Otherwise, we think most people would be better served looking to a nakiri or santoku knife. Named for the French word petite, which means small, the petty knife is often a replica of the gyuto, just in a much, much smaller form. Most petty knives are around five inches long and feature a thin, lightly curved blade with a drop point tip and heel just tall enough to keep your fingers from bashing into the cutting board. Petty knives are great utility knives for small tasks, like dicing a shallot, slicing garlic, or slicing herbs, but they’re also long and nimble enough to be great slicers. Unless you do a lot of handheld turning and peeling, a petty knife is a great replacement for a paring knife in your lineup. We found that both the MAC Professional Petty Knife and the Tojiro Classic Petty Knife were sharp enough to slice a steak while still being the perfect size to slice strawberries for your morning yogurt bowl. Traditionally a fisherman’s knife used for all sorts of purposes on the boat, the funayuki is an old-school knife shape that predates the gyuto and santoku, and it likely helped inspire both shapes. The traditional funayuki is a shorter knife, around seven inches long, with a narrow, pointed tip and a tall heel. They are santoku-sized but gyuto-shaped. Unlike the deba knife, which was a heavy, single-bevel knife used for fish butchery, the funayuki was designed to be light and nimble so that fishermen could fillet their lunch while at sea. These days, most home cooks might pick up a funayuki as a secondary, shorter gyuto, or opt for this shape over a santoku as an all-purpose utility knife with a narrower tip. Though it’s not as common in modern kitchens, one of our favorite Japanese chef’s knives is the Akiru-Saku Funayuki Gyuto, which is more traditionally shaped like a funayuki but is advertised as a gyuto since the two shapes are so similar. The kiritsuke is a Japanese slicing knife with an angular “sword tip” that allows the user to make precision cuts. The initial design combined a long slicing shape and tall heel, making the kiritsuke a hybrid knife, similar to the santoku. For most people, the kiritsuke will be a version of an all-purpose chef’s knife that could take the place of a gyuto as a daily driver, with the big difference coming in the shape of the tip. When reviewing chef’s knives, we found that the Shun Classic Kiritsuke was a great all-purpose chef’s knife with a unique tip that some people might prefer over a gyuto, since it curves upward more like a Western chef’s knife and allows for more of a rock chop motion. Boning and fillet knives are often unitaskers that don’t see much use unless you’re a fan of home butchery, but the Japanese honesuki is an even more specialized boning knife shape. Designed specifically for poultry, the honesuki is a steep, wedge-shaped knife with a very fine point and a tall heel. The goal is to have a knife that’s delicate enough to slip between a chicken joint while being sturdy enough to cut through cartilage. While the honesuki was designed for a specific purpose, we find that this shape is more versatile and can be swapped in for a petty knife for other small chopping and dicing tasks in ways that a curved fillet knife can’t. We like the MAC Professional Honesuki as a great option that could tackle most boning-knife tasks while remaining sharp and versatile enough for utility work. If you find yourself breaking down a whole chicken while also wanting a strawberry-slicing knife, the honesuki could be a nonconventional multitasker.

item.title: U.S. Air Travel Disrupted by Nationwide Ground Stop Amid Communication Outages
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler, The Points Guy
The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) imposed a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday, halting all outbound flights from the country due to a telecommunications outage. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stated there was 'no indication as of yet' that anything 'nefarious' caused the disruption, attributing it to a broad communication issue. The FAA confirmed the halt was precautionary, noting all flights had been accounted for, with international flights managed on a case-by-case basis. Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy described the stop as a response to a 'communication issue' under investigation by FAA technicians. The last nationwide ground stop occurred in January 2023 following a FAA system outage. CNBC reported the outage was linked to widespread server failures affecting telecommunications, citing internal information from Alaska Airlines. Cirium, an aviation analytics firm, noted 26,284 flights were scheduled for November 13, with 600 diverted by 5:50 p.m., 496 returning to origin airports and 104 redirected. By 4 p.m. Eastern time, 11,000 flights remained scheduled. United Airlines clarified that in-transit aircraft would continue operations, while new domestic flights were suspended. The FAA’s ground stop, which lasted several hours, led to significant disruptions, stranding travelers and forcing hundreds of flights to divert. By Saturday morning, FlightAware data showed 3,400 cancellations, with over 12,000 departures canceled since Friday. The FAA’s decision followed an equipment upgrade at air traffic control centers, marking only the second such nationwide stop since 9/11. Airlines advised passengers of refund policies under Department of Transportation rules, offering refunds for significant delays—three hours on domestic flights or six hours internationally. Alaska Air Group noted flights within Alaska and Hawaii remained operational, while West Coast-to-Hawaii departures continued. Passengers faced extended delays, with rental cars and hotel bookings near airports becoming scarce. Travelers were urged to act quickly to secure backup options, including using airline miles for rebooking. While some rewards credit cards offer trip delay protection, coverage for FAA-related disruptions is not guaranteed. The FAA lifted the ground stop late Friday, but cancellations and delays persisted into the weekend, leaving travelers to navigate the aftermath of one of the most significant disruptions in decades.
