item.title: IDEA: Follow This ‘Map of Quietude’ to the Most Silent Trails in Sweden
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
The invitation piqued my interest as soon as it landed in my inbox: “A beachfront cabin where you can stay for free,” it read, describing a remote spot on the Baltic coast in southwest Sweden. “The only condition? You have to stay quiet.” Surrounded by apple orchards, with the sea just out the door, this idyllic place would be available to a few lucky travelers—as long as we maintained an air of “quietude” during our respective stays. Outfitted with sound-measuring technology to monitor noise levels inside, the unique setup of the Stay Quiet Cabin is part of a broader initiative by Visit Skåne (pronounced skaw-nuh) to combat one of Europe’s most significant environmental health issues: noise pollution. According to the European Commission, prolonged exposure to loud, chronic noise is the second largest cause of health problems contributing to cardiovascular disease, sleep disturbances, and stress-related health concerns. Spending time in naturally quiet environments can help relieve those symptoms. Skåne is a region renowned for its restorative pastoral and seaside landscapes, unique rural culture, farm-to-table restaurants, and heritage traditions. Within it, The Map of Quietude—a list of 26 places mapped by a professional sound engineer—leads to many spots along Skåne’s 1,000+ miles of hiking trails. Each spot’s silence has been measured to ensure distinctly healing experiences. I found that pausing in them to take in the stillness and beauty added something beyond a typical travel or hiking experience. It gave me insight into the true frequency of a place and what it offers: peace, an immersion in rejuvenating slowness, and awe. After my days in silence on the coast, I’ve rounded up some best trails where you can easily experience these locations of quietude, while also taking in interesting communities, historic sites, and some of Scandinavia’s most beautiful wildernesses. Sweden’s nature-centric way of life includes the right of public access, or allemansrätten, which allows hiking or camping almost anywhere in the countryside with the expectation that you will respect the land. Part of the Öresund Way, this loop is worth a detour from inland Skåne to discover a car-free island where people come to bike and hike. You can also get some of the region’s best cardamom buns at Hven Durum, a family-run bakery and mill. A quick ferry will bring you to this tiny slip of seaside heaven. Walk along the coastline and through a species-rich nature reserve for sweeping views of the Öre Sound and Copenhagen skyline. Ven’s southern headland, södra udde, is a nature reserve and designated place of quietude. See an active, mid-20th-century lighthouse nearby. Or, check out the site of 16th-century Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe’s observatory. Distance: 7.4 Miles (bonus summit extends to 11.4 miles) Starting at the edge of the Kulla peninsula in northwest Skåne, you’ll trace roughly seven and a half miles of mostly flat shoreline south from the small fishing village Mölle. One of Sweden’s first seaside resorts at the turn of the 19th century, city dwellers came here for their nature fix. Back then, Mölle was steeped in scandal when, after long hikes, men and women began swimming together in the sea nearby, something that was unthinkable at the time. The route explores nature reserves and gnarled pine forests and winds past beaches and historic towns. You’ll even pass remains of Kulla fälad, a vast historic pasture that served as a shared grazing land for livestock for centuries. In some places, ancient drystone walls are still visible. You’ll end in Höganäs, a globally renowned center of stoneware and ceramics production. It’s also a great place to explore a burgeoning creative community. Stop by The Hub Höganäs to experience local life, where artists sell heritage-steeped crafts, and locals gather for events. If you’re looking for a great place to eat, try Hubben, a local spot run by friendly Swedes. To visit a place of Quietude, start in the spectacular Kullaberg Nature Reserve. From there, head to Håkull, the region’s highest peak. The summit offers panoramic views of the sea and Danish coastline. It will add about four miles to your trek. For over 100 miles, the Österlen Way traverses the southeast corner of Skåne. This is Sweden’s famed culinary region. It’s also where my Stay Quiet Cabin was located. Starting in the medieval town of Ystad, the Österlen Way follows the Baltic Sea coast. It passes through nature reserves, national parks, and fishing villages, with inland stretches through ancient forest. Among other fascinating stops, you’ll pass the hilltop stone circle, Ales Stenar. This is often referred to as “Sweden’s Stonehenge” for its similarly mysterious origins. The trail has two spots of Quietude. The first is Meditationsplatsen, a circular enclosure where people come to meditate. There’s also Gislövshammar Quarry, a 19th-century limestone quarry on the coast of its namesake fishing village. This area is known for its many orchards, farms, and excellent independent shops and bakeries. This breathtaking route hugs the wave-swept coastline of the Öresund Strait. From north to south, it passes through historic fishing villages and dramatic landscapes. It combines previously mentioned trails and quiet spots (Håkull, Mölle to Höganäs, and Ven Island) with two additional places of Quietude. There are the historic open-air cold bathing houses Pålsjöbaden and Hilleshögs dalar valley. Hikers pass beaches, meadows, dunes and cliffs, and enter pine forests. The trail varies in difficulty before finishing with a loop around the Falsterbonäset Peninsula. Stone Age graves, medieval castle ruins, and views of the Danish coast keep things interesting. The final legs of the trail provide ample opportunities for birdwatching. It enters nature reserves that are internationally renowned habitats for many of Northern Europe’s migratory birds. At just under 1,000 miles (1,600 km), the region’s Skåneleden trail is a long-distance route that traverses a vast amount of the countryside’s changeable terrain. You’ll encounter rocky coast, verdant forest, national parks, and nature reserves. There are also historic sites like castles and stone circles. The Skåneleden Trail is divided into seven sub-trails by geographic area. There are 148 sections (encompassing all the previously mentioned routes). Many individual sections make for great day hikes. Or, combine them for longer treks over multiple days or weeks. Several sections are near train or bus stations, making transportation easy. Basic campsites with wind shelters and bathrooms are available along the way for those seeking a longer adventure. **You can hear 60-minute field recordings of birdsong, waves, and wind from each of the places of quietude mentioned above on Visit Skåne’s website or Spotify.

item.title: REVIEW: Hydra has officially been voted the best European island – here’s why it should be on your 2027 bucket list
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Island life is as fabulous as it sounds, with a mild year-round climate, infinite coves to explore and a laid-back atmosphere. And in Europe, there are endless options to hop between. Arguably, Italy and Spain have the most beautiful array of islands on the continent, but Portugal, France and Croatia also boast some gorgeous spots worth a visit. But if there is one country whose islands capture the hearts of British holidaymakers more than any other, it's Greece. When you think of a Greek island holiday, chances are Santorini’s whitewashed houses or the beach clubs of Mykonos spring to mind first. But according to our readers, we’ve all been looking in the wrong direction. In this year’s Readers’ Choice Awards, the tiny island of Hydra was crowned the best island in Europe, scoring an impressive 98.12 and beating Mediterranean heavyweights including Sardinia, Naxos, Sicily, Mallorca and Ibiza. Greece performed particularly well in this year’s ranking, with seven islands making the top 20. But Hydra’s first-place position feels particularly fitting at a time when many of us are looking for slower, calmer holidays away from traffic, crowds and packed itineraries. Hydra doesn’t have an airport, and you won’t be needing a car when you arrive either. Motorised vehicles are largely prohibited on the island, apart from a small number used for essential services, so getting around mostly means walking or travelling by boat. Step off the ferry in Hydra Town and you’re met by an amphitheatre of stone houses rising above a horseshoe-shaped harbour, where fishing boats and yachts bob beside waterfront cafés and narrow, cobbled streets climb into the hills behind. In a world where we're constantly trying to get somewhere faster, Hydra's greatest luxury might be that it forces you to slow down. Days can be spent walking along coastal paths, stopping for long lunches by the water and cooling off in the brilliantly clear Aegean. You won't find endless stretches of powdery sand here, but that's part of the charm. Spilia, just outside Hydra Town, is a favourite spot for diving straight from the rocks, while the charming villages of Kamini and Vlychos are within walking distance of the main port. More secluded coves and beaches can easily be reached by water taxi. Hydra has long attracted people looking to escape everyday life. In the 1950s and 1960s, the island became a magnet for an international community of artists and writers, most famously Leonard Cohen, who bought a house here in 1960 and spent several years on the island. For such a small island, there's plenty of history, too. Hydra played an important role in the Greek War of Independence, thanks largely to its powerful maritime fleet, and its seafaring past can be explored at the Historical Archives Museum of Hydra beside the harbour. Perhaps most appealingly, Hydra feels remote without actually being particularly difficult to reach. Ferries from Piraeus connect Athens with the island in as little as around an hour and 30 minutes, depending on the service, making it easy to combine a few slow days here with a city break in the eclectic Greek capital. Hydra certainly isn't a secret, and summer brings plenty of visitors to its little harbour. But its lack of cars and large-scale development has helped preserve a sense of place that can be harder to find on some of the Mediterranean's most popular islands. For 2027, that might be reason enough to put Europe's newly crowned number one on your bucket list. The best islands in Europe, according to you in the 2026 Readers' Choice Awards

item.title: Half Cruise, Half Cargo Ship? What It's Like to Sail French Polynesia Aboard a Local Freighter
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
It’s certainly a romantic notion to hop a freighter and sail to the distant South Pacific. One could spend days at sea staring at nothing but seabirds and cargo pallets, waking up to the sound of those pallets being offloaded onto a tiny concrete wharf, meeting a community nestled among palms. One could take the day to hike or tour the island, or feast on fresh catches with the locals, while the offloaded pallets are filled with grapefruits, dried coconut husks, and flowers to be sold elsewhere—Tahiti, perhaps. It might come as a surprise to know that one company has been offering dedicated cruises built around that very premise for over 40 years. In French Polynesia, the locally owned cruise line Aranui Cruises offers combination passenger and cargo services from Papeete, Tahiti, to the dramatically jagged volcanic pitons and pastoral scenes of the Marquesas Islands. The idea is simple: a ship operates a cargo service to the remote islands (two of them, Fatu Hiva and Tahuata, have no airport and are only accessible by sea), and while the inbound cargo of soft drinks, groceries, building supplies, and even racing canoes is unloaded in the port, the passengers can use the time to go touring. In March 2026, I joined one such sailing, onboard the purpose-built Aranui V to see exactly what the 12-night, nearly-thousand-mile journey to the Marquesas looks like. I like to refer to the vessel as the “mullet ship”— cargo up front, cruise in the back. During the voyage, when I wasn’t swimming in the onboard pool, or enjoying a cocktail from the bar, I filled my days with lectures Dr. Carole S. Ivory, professor emerita from Washington State University, who specializes in the study of Marquesan culture and art. I got to witness that culture up close on Aranui’s included shore excursions. The experiences were visits to archaeological sites and volcanic pitons by car on Nuku Hiva, or various organized hikes on several of the other islands. There are also optional excursions for an additional fee, like the scenic drive between two sides of the island on Fatu Hiva. The drive, which traced a narrow mountain road between villages, offered spectacular vistas from the sea cliffs and, to rejoin the ship, a bonus sunset barge ride—a worthy add-on. Local residents hired by Aranui guide passengers in their personal cars as these tiny islands have no buses. On tiny Ua Huka, our mahu driver (a person of third-gender common in Polynesia) wearing a red flowered dress and straw hat, spent the day chatting with passengers and eating. And oh, how we ate! Baguette sandwiches during a morning stop at a craft center. A plate of chow mein from the snack bar at the botanical garden. A tour-of-the-island plate from the buffet heaped with coconut milk-roasted goat, the raw fish salad poisson cru, steamed taro, rice, and magenta-colored mashed banana swimming in sweet condensed coconut milk. On each of the islands, we passengers from the Aranui V were greeted with local musicians and artisans, typically in a community pavilion. The Marquesas are noted for their skilled carvers, working in both wood and bone to create intricately decorated bowls, decorative canoe paddles, and jewelry. Carvers also work in stone called te ke’a pua (flower stone), also known as garnet phonolite, a polished volcanic rock that has the natural appearance of being covered in crystalline flowers. The rocks themselves are found on the island of Ua Pou, and are worked into a variety of shapes: ornamental fish hooks, decorative whales and birds, and pestles used to smash taro called kea tuki popoi. Unlike most cruise lines, which have multinational crews, Aranui instead runs a local cargo service that just happens to have a large international tourism component. This means all of the onboard crew are Polynesians, many of them originally from the Marquesas themselves. The service is friendly and informal, and I was often greeted on a first-name basis. A couple of the crew recognized me from my previous sailing to another island group, already some four years hence. Aranui also doesn’t enforce the same separation between passengers and crew that is prevalent on other ships—passengers and crew can freely mingle. After dinner, many crew members and officers end up in the bar for nightcaps right alongside the passengers. On my previous voyage with Aranui, to the Austral Islands, I joined an impromptu card game in the onboard pearl boutique and watched the head of housekeeping handily clean out the ship’s captain over the course of several hands of poker, all while we and the silken strands of Tahitian Pearls in the display cases bore witness. When my only pair of sandals broke alighting from the landing craft on Ua Huka, Aranui staff directed me to the ship’s French doctor, who fixed it with tape from his medical bag. “Come back later onboard,” he said, “and we’ll do surgery on the shoe.” While I waited, I took great amusement with a large notice on the door of the ship’s infirmary, warning that many of the fruits served onboard and in the islands have “diuretic and laxatif (sp) effect,” urging passengers to consume in moderation. I wondered how many passengers had visited the infirmary over the years with the same complaint before they felt the need to put up a sign. At the end of our stop on Ua Huka, we all gathered on the deck of Aranui V. We still had calls on the islands of Rangiroa and Bora Bora scheduled, but it was time to bid our goodbyes to the Marquesas in a traditional manner. A member of the onboard staff invoked a prayer of thanks for the voyage and fond farewell to these magnificent islands, which we did with armfuls of local flowers and plants cast into sunset-dappled sea to watch float ashore. That, however, wasn’t the lasting image of the Marquesas for me. For weeks after my trip, I awoke each morning in a home that seemed suddenly foreign, recalling the smell of the straw hats, the taste of the baked banana, the green of the mountains, the red floral dress of the snacking mahu, and the pallets of coconuts and grapefruits stacked on the tiny wharf.

item.title: IDEA: 9 Chefs on the Meals They're Traveling For in 2027—From Korean Soups to Peruvian Ceviche
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Any professional chef can confirm that while menu development, staffing, interior design, and operations are all part of running a restaurant or kitchen, finding the time to travel in search of different flavors often feels like a rare luxury. But spending time in a different city or region is key to staying inspired. Even a quick weekend getaway can lead to incorporating new ingredients in familiar dishes, serve as an opportunity to learn a new culinary technique, help forge a connection with one’s own heritage, or connect with peers who are pushing the industry forward. As the end of the calendar year draws near, we spoke with some of our favorite women chefs about where they’re most excited to visit in 2027—from a sushi counter in Tokyo to the oldest restaurant in Beirut—and what they’re hoping to eat and learn from those travels. Foraged foods in the Basque Country, Spain “I went [to the Basque Country] for the first time in 2013, but it was such a quick, rushed trip that I left feeling like I’d barely scratched the surface. I’ve been wanting to go back and really do it right ever since. At the top of my list of spots is Arrea!, Edorta Lamo’s restaurant in Kanpezu, a small village in the mountains of Álava. I’ve heard such wonderful things about it. What excites me is that it’s not the Basque Country most people think of first—as in, San Sebastián with its coastline and all of its pintxo bars. It’s inland cooking, built on what’s hunted, foraged, and grown right there in the mountains. And I'll be eating my way through plenty of pintxo bars too, of course. — Katie Button, chef/co-founder of Cúrate Bar de Tapas in Asheville, and author of Spanish Accent cookbook Soft polenta at The Lost Kitchen in Freedom, Maine “I’m in love with Erin French’s new cookbook [Seize the Supper], and wildly enough, Maine is one of the few states I've never been to. So, I'm plotting something for next summer. I love that it's a mostly female crew, a standout (unfortunately) in our industry. Erin’s focus on local produce and connecting to the earth speaks to my own regenerative cooking and inspires me constantly to dig deeper and deeper. I also admire her ethos of humble simplicity, distilling dishes to their core, filled with soul and properly honoring ingredients, with a nod to her family's heritage. I dream of her play on sweet and savory—like the soft polenta with honey and ricotta.” — Camilla Marcus, chef and founder of Westbourne “I am most looking forward to traveling to Boulder to visit my friends Kelly Jeun and Eduardo Vallelobo at their restaurant Casa Juani. Both are accomplished chefs who are experts in Italian and Spanish cuisines, and they recently made Bon Appétit's Best New Restaurants list. I am most excited to try everything on their menu, which is entirely Spanish. Eduardo is very proud of—and from!—Madrid, and the menu celebrates Spanish cuisine and culture.” —Melissa Rodriguez, Chef & Partner at Crane Club & Bar CC in New York City “[Sushi Meino], a six-seat counter in Tokyo’s Azabujuban neighborhood by Chef Mei Kougo, one of only a few female sushi masters in Japan, has been high on my list since it opened in 2023 and I haven’t yet had the luck of securing a very-difficult-to-get reservation. I'm heading back to Tokyo in the spring and hoping 2027 will be my year! If I don’t get in, I’ll still be heading to Makimaki, her takeout-only hosomaki shop that opened nearby earlier this year.” — Rebekah Peppler, recipe developer and author Temple food in Jangseong County, South Korea “Eating at venerable Jeong Kwan’s table has been high on my list for years, and I was devastated to be out of town when she and Chef Esu Lee were cooking together at his excellent restaurant Orson in Paris recently. It lit a fire in me to finally prioritize booking a trip to Baekyangsa Temple [where she cooks] to attend one of her demonstrations in 2027.” — R.P. “I'm dying to try manakish and shawarma straight from the source. Plus ka'ak, the ring-shaped street bread with sesame, along with all the spreads from the market. And [I want to pay a] visit to El Soussi, one of Beirut's oldest restaurants, famous for its Lebanese breakfast, especially msabbaha, the warm mashed chickpeas with lemon and tahini. I'd be sure to get an order of beid ghanam as well, which is lambs testicles cooked in lemon and olive oil, served with fattet hummus. Growing up in the US with Lebanese heritage, we often ate many Lebanese meals as a family. But the dishes we prepared and enjoyed were such a small sliver of everything Lebanon has to offer. I've been wanting to go for such a long time so I could experience the vastness of this incredible cuisine and the country's beauty. I was meant to travel there this past March, which was postponed, so it's top of my list for 2027!” —Chef Mary Attea, executive chef of Musket Room and Raf’s in New York City “I’m especially excited to explore Nikkei cuisine and experience Peruvian ceviche firsthand. In Mexico, we make wonderful ceviches, but I believe Peruvians have truly mastered the art of preparing this dish. I want to experience their approach to seafood, acidity, and flavor in its place of origin, while exploring the broader culinary traditions of Peru. I believe there are many shared histories and points of connection between Latin American cultures that we don’t always recognize, and I want to explore those connections through food. I’m also drawn to the opportunity to experience traditional Mesoamérican markets that are still operating throughout Peru, not only in Lima but in other regions as well. Markets reveal so much about a place: its ingredients, its people, its traditions, and the ways food connects communities. I’d also love to experience Inca culture firsthand and better understand the country’s rich cultural and culinary heritage.” —Norma Listman, chef and co-founder, Masala y Maíz in Mexico City “I’m particularly interested in Assam’s distinctive use of black sesame and wild greens. During a trip to Mumbai, I had the opportunity to taste Assamese food prepared by two sisters who cook and preserve traditional Assamese foodways. Their food completely blew my mind. I would love to travel to Assam to learn more about the region’s culinary traditions and experience its food culture firsthand. As a chef who cooks both Indian and Mexican cuisine, I feel a responsibility to keep learning and exploring the vastness and richness of India’s food traditions. India is incredibly diverse, and there is still so much for me to discover. Now, as the mother of a mixed child with Indian heritage, I feel an even greater responsibility to expose him to his culture. Traveling to Assam would be an opportunity to continue learning for myself while creating a meaningful connection between my son and his cultural roots.” — N.L. “I hosted a pop-up at ADI last year, and was able to witness firsthand the ways in which chef Kanchan [Adhikari] is doing the most incredibly inventive things with food within the South Asian diaspora while also marrying it with a Japanese omakase-style sentiment. One of my favorite restaurants of the past year and I am counting down the days until I can eat a meal in that gorgeous dining room again!"” —Samah Dada, chef and creator of recipe platform DADA Eats “Inje is the smallest county in South Korea and is most famous for hwangtae guk (dried pollock) soup. You can find many restaurants clustered together there that serve this regional specialty, but my absolute favorite is a place called Song-yi Sikdang. The brief menu basically comes down to the hwangtae jungsik—a set that includes pollock soup, a whole grilled pollock, an assortment of 12 perfectly seasoned namul banchans, and a warm bowl of rice. Inje is located in the Taebaek mountains alongside rivers and basins, so when you get there, you’re surrounded by stunning landscape and flora, which is absolutely gorgeous year round—ranging from verdant mountains, to golden and crimson foliage, to snowy tree tops. Inje is a short and tranquil two-hour drive from Seoul and feels similar to that of driving upstate on the Taconic from Manhattan. The geography and climate makes it the perfect environment for preparing dried pollock and also foraging for diverse wild greens and herbs (namuls), rare ones that you can only find there and are seasonally available at local farmers markets. —Clara Lee, co-author of Korean Soups and co-founder of food company Queens Fresh fish and handmade pasta in Puglia, Italy I have been wanting to travel to Italy for many years, and Puglia has been top of mind. It feels like a place where food is still very much connected to the culture and deeply rooted in the abundance of the land. Since the provenance of things is our ethos, this feels particularly aligned for me. Anytime I travel (but specifically Europe). “I am really drawn to the simplicity of the cuisine. A beautiful local grilled fish with olive oil, handmade pasta, regional cheeses—these are all things that truly excite me as a chef because their beauty is in how uncomplicated they are. Local, fresh bounty, cooked well: to me this is what makes food memorable.” —Abigail Dahan-Kramer, pastry chef at Provenance in Philadelphia

item.title: INSTRUCTION: How to Make the Most of a Weekend City Break
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Picture the end of a long work week. You are tired, your inbox is full, and your mind is still buzzing. Then you step off a train in a new city. The air smells different, the streets are unfamiliar, and for the first time in days, your shoulders drop. Even a short trip can reset the mind. New sights, sounds, and a different daily rhythm give your brain a break from routine. If you want to build calm, mindful habits for every trip, Overwell offers simple tools to help you slow down and notice what matters. The key idea is this: a weekend away works best when planned with care but lived with curiosity and calm. Before you book anything, ask yourself one simple question: "What do I want to feel this weekend?" The answer shapes everything that follows. Some people want deep rest after a hard season. Others want adventure, art, good food, or quiet time with someone they love. Knowing your purpose helps you choose the right city, pace, and activities. If you want rest, a small walkable town with cozy cafés may suit you better than a large capital with long lines. This step also protects you from a common trap: trying to do everything. When we do not know what we want, we try to see every sight and end the trip more tired than when we began. A clear intention is like a compass. It keeps you from drifting into stress. A Light Plan With Space for the Unexpected Good planning does not mean filling every hour. It means making a few smart choices so the rest of the trip can flow. Start with where you stay. A place in a walkable area saves time and energy because you can step outside and explore without long rides. Next, pick a few places you truly want to see. Two or three is often enough for a short stay. If a spot is popular, like a famous museum or well-known restaurant, book ahead so you do not waste time waiting in line. Then leave open time in your days, hours with no plan at all. This balance matters. Too many plans create stress and make the trip feel like a task list. Too few can lead to wasted hours and the feeling that you missed out. A gentle middle path gives you structure free of pressure. You know where you are going but still have space for surprises, like a street musician, a secret garden, or a friendly local who points you toward a favorite bakery. Famous landmarks are worth a visit, but a city's soul often hides in ordinary places. To really feel a place, experience its everyday life. Walk through a residential neighborhood where people are following their daily routines. Visit a local market and see what people buy. Sit in a small café and taste what locals eat for breakfast. These acts help you feel the city's real rhythm. You begin to notice how people greet each other, how fast they walk, and what they enjoy during a quiet afternoon. Imagine spending a slow morning on a bench near a small square. You sip a warm drink and watch the world pass by. Children run after pigeons, an older man reads his newspaper, and a couple laughs over a shared pastry. Nothing special happens, yet this moment may stay in your memory longer than any famous monument. Small moments often become the best memories. Staying Present and Protecting Your Energy Travel can pull us out of the moment in surprising ways. We take endless photos, check our phones, and feel pressure to see everything. Soon we are looking at the city through a screen instead of with our own eyes. Try putting your phone away for a few hours. Notice the sounds of the street, the smell of hot bread, the shade of old buildings in late light. When you pay attention this way, even a simple walk feels rich. Your mind settles, and the memory sticks more deeply. It is just as vital to listen to your own energy. Cities can be loud and busy, and walking all day is tiring. Make time for good meals, regular breaks, and enough sleep. A slower pace is not a waste. It lets you enjoy what you do see. Remember that skipping an attraction to rest is not failure. It is a wise choice. You came to refresh yourself, not to win a prize for seeing the most sights. If your body asks for a quiet hour in a park, give it that gift. When the weekend ends, you do not have to leave the good feeling behind. A few small steps can help you carry it home. On the way back, take quiet minutes to reflect. Ask yourself, "What moments made me smile? What did I learn about what I need?" You might write down your favorite recollections in a notebook or a note on your phone. You can also choose one small habit from the journey to keep. Maybe it is an evening walk, a slow morning coffee, or a new way of exploring your own neighborhood. In the end, a weekend city break is not about how much you see. It is about how deeply you feel. A few mindful days away can refresh your mind, soften your stress, and leave you feeling lighter long after you return. This story was published in partnership with Overwell.

item.title: A Teen Rescuer Helped Save a Lost Senior Hiker with FaceTime Tech Support
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Marin County Search and Rescue volunteers escort an 88-year-old hiker through Mount Burdell Preserve in Northern California after locating her on November 10 with help from a teenage volunteer who used FaceTime to retrieve her GPS coordinates. (Photo: Marin County Search and Rescue) A 17-year-old search-and-rescue volunteer helped locate a lost 88-year-old hiker in Northern California after conventional cellphone-tracking methods failed. The volunteer rescuer, named Cody Davis, eventually used FaceTime to take control of the hiker’s iPhone screen and retrieve her GPS coordinates. “I’m not a super tech person,” Davis told Outside. “But I’m young, and it’s easy for us to figure stuff like that out.” The woman was found uninjured on November 10 at Mount Burdell Preserve, near Novato, California, after becoming separated from her hiking companions. Molly Williams, operations director for Marin County Search and Rescue, told Outside that the woman had gotten off the trail and headed downhill, although it remains unclear how the separation happened. Her companions tried unsuccessfully to locate her before calling for help. Around 50 members of Marin County Search and Rescue mobilized to search the preserve. Williams, who oversaw the operation, said rescuers received the call around 2 P.M. and located the woman around 4 P.M. A report of the rescue mission was published on the Marin County Search and Rescue group’s Facebook page. Davis, a high school senior, was among the first search and rescue volunteers to arrive on the scene. According to Williams, Marin County’s search-and-rescue team accepts volunteers as young as 14. “Probably a third or more of our members are high school age, and they are full members,” Williams said. “They respond in the same ways as the adults.” Before rescuers arrived, 911 dispatchers had also tried and failed to pinpoint the missing hiker’s position by phone. When Davis got to the command post, he called her to ask about her surroundings, but Mount Burdell’s rolling hills and scattered trees offered few distinguishing landmarks. Attempts to track her through CalTopo, a search-and-rescue mapping platform, and Apple’s Find My Friends feature were also unsuccessful. Davis eventually connected with the woman over FaceTime and asked her to show him the terrain. When that didn’t help, he remembered hearing that newer versions of FaceTime allowed users to remotely control another person’s iPhone screen with permission. “I was able to remotely access her screen, which was weird,” Davis told Outside. “I’d never done that before, but I just sorta figured it out.” At that point, Davis had already spent roughly an hour and a half on the phone with the hiker, he told Outside. Their calls kept dropping, and although the woman was unfamiliar with some of her phone’s features, she worked with Davis as he patiently explained each step. “She was great, and was as helpful as she could be, being unfamiliar with the device,” Davis said. “She was a good sport.” As darkness approached and the hiker’s phone battery drained, Davis managed to access her screen, adjust several location settings, and retrieve her GPS coordinates using the Maps and Compass apps. He immediately relayed them to search teams in the field. Williams credited Davis’s persistence with helping searchers reach the woman sooner. “The searchers would have found her eventually, but we found her a lot faster because Cody figured that out,” she said. Shortly after Davis relayed the hiker’s coordinates, their call disconnected again. By the time he reconnected over FaceTime, rescuers had located the woman. “I called her back just as teams were approaching, and we all saw the moment the first team made contact with her while she was on FaceTime,” Davis said. “It was ultimately a cool experience.” Rescuers helped the woman return to the trail, and Williams said she walked out with them in good spirits. Williams urged hikers to stay with their companions, particularly when members of a group move at different speeds. If you lose your bearings, Davis advised staying on established trails rather than heading downhill in hopes of finding a road or another path. Search teams typically check trails first, he explained, and leaving them makes it harder for rescuers to find you. He also recommended that hikers learn how to retrieve GPS coordinates from a phone’s Maps or Compass app before heading out, so they can relay their location directly to emergency responders. Ultimately, Williams pointed to several advantages the woman had when she lost her way. She carried a charged phone, had cell service, and answered when rescuers called. “Often when we get called for a search, somebody doesn’t call until their phone is dying, or they’ve used their flashlight for so long that the phone is dying,” she said. Starting out with a charged phone and knowing how to share coordinates can make all the difference when a routine hike takes a wrong turn.
